t: LeetCode 1357 — Apply Discount Every n Orders
o: We maintain a supermarket catalog (product ID → price) and a customer counter. Each `getBill` call computes the subtotal by summing `amount[j] * price(product[j])`, increments the counter, and applies a percentage discount only when the counter is a multiple of `n`. In Example 1, calls 1, 2, 4, 5, 7 pay full price; calls 3 and 6 are every-3rd customers and get 50% off (1600→800, 14700→7350). Constraints are tiny (≤200 products, ≤1000 calls), so any straightforward lookup structure works; the only real design decision is how to map product IDs to prices quickly.
k: A hash map from product ID to price gives O(1) lookups per item in each bill.
Track a running customer count and apply the discount exactly when count % n == 0.
Compute the subtotal as an integer, then multiply by (100 - discount) / 100 as floating point to avoid precision issues.

a.i: For each item in a bill, scan the `products` array to find its index and read the corresponding price. With at most 200 products and 1000 calls of up to 200 items, this is at most ~40 million operations — fast enough for the given limits, though not scalable.
s: Store n, discount, products, and prices as instance fields.
On getBill, increment the counter and compute subtotal by linear-searching each product ID in products to get its price.
If counter % n == 0, return subtotal * (100 - discount) / 100.0; otherwise return subtotal as double.
a.t: O(P × B) per bill, where P is catalog size (≤200) and B is bill size (≤200) — linear search per item dominates.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond storing the input arrays.

a.i: Precompute a dictionary mapping each product ID to its price once in the constructor. Every lookup during `getBill` is then O(1), making each bill O(B). This is the natural design-class solution: build the index once, query many times.
s: In the constructor, build a hash map {product ID → price} and store n, discount, and a counter set to 0.
Sum amount[j] * priceMap[product[j]] over all j to get the integer subtotal.
If counter % n == 0, return subtotal * (100 - discount) / 100.0; else return subtotal as a double.
a.t: O(P) constructor to build the map, O(B) per getBill — constant-time lookups per item.

w: Pick Approach 2 in an interview — it demonstrates the standard 'preprocess once, query fast' design pattern that these Design-tag problems test. Common pitfalls: forgetting to increment the counter on every call including non-discounted ones; applying the discount based on the wrong multiple (use `count % n == 0`); integer overflow of the subtotal in C++/Java (max ~200×200×1000×1000 fits comfortably in a 64-bit long); and returning an int instead of a double. Edge cases: n = 1 means every customer gets the discount; discount = 0 changes nothing. Likely follow-ups: support changing n or discount at runtime (trivial field updates), or handle bills with duplicate product entries (accumulate amounts first or just sum all lines).
